questions: Did the shaking substantially lessen or stop when you were distracted or concentrating on another task?
Could the shaking be made to match the rhythm of a voluntary movement in another limb?
Did the shaking begin suddenly rather than gradually?
Did the shaking return or worsen after zonisamide was stopped or reduced?
Did it improve after zonisamide was restarted?
Is the shaking present when your arms are completely relaxed?
Is it worse when maintaining a posture or performing an action than when resting?
Does it fluctuate markedly from one moment or task to another?
Do you experience similar jerking or shaking in your legs, head, voice, or trunk?
Do you have episodes of loss of awareness, staring, or unresponsiveness?
Have you ever had a convulsion or been diagnosed with epilepsy?
Do you experience sudden brief jerks of the arms or other body parts?
Did the abnormal movements begin after an injury, illness, major stress, or change in medication?
Do you have weakness, numbness, imbalance, slowness, or stiffness?
Does alcohol temporarily reduce the shaking?
Does anyone in your family have a similar tremor or other movement disorder?
Are you currently taking any medication besides zonisamide that can affect movement?
Have you had normal brain imaging or neurological testing for this problem?

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Probable corticobasal syndrome due to an underlying 4-repeat tauopathy, most likely corticobasal degeneration, presenting with cortical myoclonus (irregular postural tremor), asymmetric parkinsonism, and frontal executive dysfunction  
ALTERNATIVE: Progressive supranuclear palsy (4-repeat tauopathy)  
ALTERNATIVE: Dementia with Lewy bodies with parkinsonism and myoclonus  
ALTERNATIVE: Neurological Wilson disease due to ATP7B-related copper accumulation despite currently nondiagnostic serum copper studies
